newsitem.title: KENYA: Somali warlords agree to end fighting, Kenya says.
newsitem.headline: Somali warlords agree to end fighting, Kenya says.

text.p: Somali warlords on Tuesday declared an end to hostilities in their devastated country at the end of a week of talks at the invitation of Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi, the Kenyan government said.

The leaders, who included Hussein Aideed and Ali Mahdi Mohamed, agreed to allow free movement of people in Mogadishu and to remove all roadblocks leading from one region to another in the divided Somali capital, the government said in a statement.

It was not immediately known whether Aideed, a 34-year-old former U.S. marine who took over from his father Mohamed Farah Aideed following his death in Mogadishu in August, and Ali Mahdi held a face-to-face meeting.

But suggesting that there had been round-table talks, the statement referred to President Moi opening the meeting with the message that the presence of the Somali leaders in Kenya signified their intent and seriousness in seeking peace.

"The President appealed to the Somali leaders to consider that for the last six years Somalia has had no internationally recognised government and that there has been a lot of suffering by the Somali people, especially women and children," it said.
The statement added that Moi encouraged the Somali leaders to open lines of communication and "talk amongst themselves".
Aideed, like his father, was elected president of Somalia by supporters and heads a government. But it has not received international recognition and is rejected by Ali Mahdi and other leaders.
The Kenyan government statement said the Somali leaders came to the following understanding:
- Declared cessation of hostilities, including media propaganda with immediate effect.
- Allow free movement of people in the capital Mogadishu and remove all roadblocks leading from one region to another.
- Facilitate humanitarian delivery of aid to the people of Somalia.
- Pledged continued dialogue in Somalia for a peace process and preserve the unity, sovereignity and the territorial integrity of Somalia.

The statement said the Somalis strongly rejected any attempt to initiate bilateral negotiations that may detract, divert attention from or undermine the Somali people and urged the international community to support their peace efforts.
The faction led by Hassan Ali Osman Atto, once the financier of the senior Aideed, was also represented. Other smaller groupings were also at the Nairobi talks described by diplomats as exploratory.
The Somali talks led on from Moi's intervention to secure the release on October 3 of an Australian pilot held in a jail in the southwestern Somali town of Baidoa for 131 days, diplomats said.

In a move that surprised many western diplomats in Nairobi, Moi stepped in and personally urged Aideed to free 24-year-old Australian Justin Frazer, who had been sentenced to 25 years in jail for landing his plane in Somalia without clearance in May.

The death of Mohamed Farah Aideed prompted widespread hopes in Mogadishu of a possible negotiated end to Somalia's civil war which has raged since the fall of late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991.
But south Mogadishu has been hit in the past few weeks by a series of assassinations which Somali experts say are part of a vendetta between factions to avenge Farah Aideed's death.

Moi has been closely involved in several earlier diplomatic initiatives to build peace in Somalia, including a face-to-face meeting in Nairobi between Ali Mahdi and Mohamed Farah Aideed in 1994, but they all failed to stop the fighting.
